speaker: Doctor
text: Welcome to the clinic. I see you are presenting with wrist pain, fever, and skin lesions; let's start by determining how long you have had these symptoms. When did the fever and rash first appear relative to the onset of your wrist pain?

speaker: Patient
text: 17-year-old male. The patient presents with a 3-day history of pain in his left wrist, which worsened this morning accompanied by chills and malaise. He recounts having a self-resolving left knee pain the previous week. Reports recent return from a camping trip in Minnesota. Sexually active with one female partner. No history of trauma to the wrist.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for the details. Given your recent camping trip in Minnesota and self-resolving knee pain, we must rule out Lyme disease or Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever. Can you describe the appearance of your skin lesions, and have you noticed any tick bites?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Pain in the left wrist. I also have Chills, Malaise, Painless violaceous vesiculopustular lesions on both wrists and hands, Swelling and erythema of the left wrist, Severe tenderness to palpation and passive movement of the left wrist.

speaker: Doctor
text: The description of painless violaceous vesiculopustular lesions on your wrists and hands is highly characteristic of a specific arthropod-borne infection. Given your history of camping in Minnesota and the preceding self-resolving knee pain, are you certain you have not had a tick bite on your legs or groin?

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: Otherwise healthy with no significant past medical history. Social history: Admits to being sexually active with one female partner who uses a diaphragm for contraception. Recently went on a camping trip to Minnesota.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Lyme Arthritis (caused by Borrelia burgdorferi). The combination of recent Minnesota camping, a preceding self-resolving monoarticular knee effusion, and now a swollen, tender wrist with systemic symptoms (fever, chills) and characteristic skin findings is highly suggestive of disseminated Lyme disease. I do not need any further tests to confirm this clinical diagnosis based on the classic presentation.
